children.text: A highland city on a ridge at about

elevation, 3–5 degrees cooler than Manila, with Taal Lake and the volcano inside it spread out below. With steaming bulalo, view cafes, and the Sky Ranch Ferris wheel, it's Manila's most popular weekend getaway.
Tagaytay is a highland city in Cavite province, about
60km
south of Manila. It stretches along the northern rim ridge of the massive Taal caldera, sitting at

elevation with an average annual temperature of 22–24°C, roughly 3–5 degrees cooler than Manila. Thanks to this pleasant climate, it has long been known as the "Philippines' second summer capital" and has served as a weekend retreat for Manila residents.

The star of Tagaytay is the view spread out before it: Taal Lake and Taal Volcano. Taal Lake is a caldera lake formed hundreds of thousands of years ago by a massive eruption, and the volcanic island rising from its center is one of the most active volcanoes in the Philippines. Famous for its unique geography — "a volcanic lake within an island within a lake" — this spectacular scene can be enjoyed comfortably from ridge-top viewpoints and cafe windows.
After Taal Volcano erupted in
January 2020

, the whole volcanic island was designated a permanent danger zone, and tours that once landed on the island and rode horses up to the crater are now banned. Still, the view from the Tagaytay side remains superb, and the city itself has plenty to enjoy — view cafes and restaurants, garden-style resorts, an amusement park, and a monastery.

A day trip from Manila is possible, but staying overnight lets you enjoy the cool evening air and the misty morning lake view as well — we recommend it. It suits families, couples, long-term residents worn out by the heat, and anyone who loves food and cafe hopping. Many Korean expatriates live here too, so Korean restaurants and Korean-run lodging are easy to find.
The Tagaytay Ridge runs about
32km
from
Mount Batulao
in the west to Mount Sungay in the east, and Mount Sungay at its eastern end (
above sea level) is the highest point in Cavite. Tagaytay became a city on
under Commonwealth Act No. 338, and it grew into a resort town together with the Taal Vista Lodge (today's Taal Vista Hotel), which opened on the ridge in
as President Quezon had envisioned. On
February 3, 1945
, the U.S. 11th Airborne Division parachuted onto this ridge to join the operation to retake Manila. Today it is a city of about 88,000 people (
), and every Christmas season and Holy Week it fills with vacationers escaping the heat and pilgrims visiting its convents and retreat houses.

blocks.title: Watch Taal Volcano from a ridge-top view cafe

children.text: Along the Tagaytay–Nasugbu highway, cafes and restaurants line the cliff facing the lake. Between
8 and 10 AM
, the morning mist clears to reveal the volcano clearly — the best time for the view.

A soup of beef shank bones and marrow, corn, and cabbage simmered for hours, it's the signature dish of cool Tagaytay. The restaurant row around Mahogany Market is famous as a bulalo street where the eateries use fresh beef.
Ride the "Sky Eye," a Ferris wheel about
tall, for an aerial view of Taal Lake and the volcano. It's a small amusement park, great for spending half a day with kids.
A park on the summit of Mount Sungay (about
above sea level), about
8km
east of the city center. In
, the Marcos government began building the "Palace in the Sky" to host U.S. President Reagan, who was due to visit in
; when the visit was canceled, only the bare structure remained, and after the People Power Revolution of
it became a public park. On clear days you can see Taal Lake, Laguna Lake, and even Manila Bay. From the parking lot to the summit, walk about
uphill or take the shuttle jeepney.

A park in Sungay East along the Tagaytay–Calamba Road, with viewing decks, a zipline, horseback riding, and a forest walking path (eco trail). Hut shelters line the lakeside slope, perfect for spreading out a packed lunch and resting as you look down on the lake. Admission is
per person (free for children 4 and under), and a round-trip zipline ride costs about
on weekdays and about
on weekends.

The convent chapel of the Holy Spirit Adoration Sisters, nicknamed the "Pink Sisters" for their pink habits, where the nuns take turns beside the altar behind a grille, keeping up adoration of the Blessed Sacrament without pause. Visitors write down their prayer intentions, leave them with the sisters, and spend some quiet time before leaving. Mass is at
Monday–Saturday and at
and
on Sundays; you cannot enter the chapel in sleeveless tops or shorts.
Tagaytay and nearby Alfonso have many garden-style restaurants using organic vegetables. On your way back, pick up buko pie (coconut pie), Tagaytay coffee beans, honey, and fresh pineapple as gifts.
Opened as the "Taal Vista Lodge" on
October 7, 1939

, it is considered the second-oldest hotel in the Philippines after the Manila Hotel. Set at the end of the ridge, its lawn garden and viewing deck face Taal Volcano head-on, and it sits right next to Sky Ranch and its giant Ferris wheel. Even if you're not staying, you can enjoy the view over the weekend lunch buffet at its restaurant Veranda or at the cafe.

6 AM
on weekends without fail)

On weekend afternoons, traffic on Aguinaldo Highway can stretch the ride to Manila to more than
3 hours
, so it's best to leave Tagaytay before
4 PM
at the latest.
From the PITX (integrated bus terminal) in Parañaque or terminals around Pasay Buendia/EDSA in Manila, take a bus bound for Tagaytay or Nasugbu. Travel time is about
1 hour 30 minutes–3 hours
depending on traffic, and fares are about
. Tell the driver in advance which stop you want, such as "Rotonda" or "Olivarez."
Bus companies: San Agustin, Saint Anthony Padua, TAS Trans, DLTB, and others run from PITX toward Mendez, Alfonso, and Nasugbu, passing Rotonda, Olivarez, and Mahogany Market.
Operating hours: the first bus leaves around
4–5 AM
and the last around
7–9 PM
, varying by company and terminal.
Since
September 28, 2026
, provincial bus fares have gone up, with air-conditioned buses now charging
per km. Check the latest fares before you go.
For the return trip, catch a bus to PITX or Buendia in front of Olivarez Plaza or at a stop on Aguinaldo Highway near Rotonda.
By Grab from central Manila, it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
and costs about
one way. Since it can be hard to get a Grab back from Tagaytay, many travelers book a chartered van with driver (about
per day, depending on whether fuel and tolls are included).
It's about
60km
from Manila, and three routes are commonly used. The easiest is to exit the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) at Santa Rosa and drive up the Santa Rosa–Tagaytay Road (about
23km

); you can also switch from SLEX to the Cavite–Laguna Expressway (CALAX) and take the Silang (Aguinaldo) exit onto Aguinaldo Highway. Aguinaldo Highway, which runs from the Cavite Expressway (CAVITEX) through Bacoor, Imus, and Dasmariñas, has many traffic lights and frequent congestion. The drive takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
on weekdays and can take
3 hours
or more on weekends and holidays.

items.title: From the airports and other regions

children.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA): Take an airport bus, taxi, or Grab from the airport to PITX (
20–40 minutes
), then transfer to a bus bound for Tagaytay.
Clark International Airport: Since
March 17, 2026
, Genesis has run direct buses between Clark Airport and PITX eight times a day. The ride takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
; the fare was
when the service launched, but P2P bus fares rose 15% on
September 28, 2026
, so check before boarding.
From Batangas: Buses from Nasugbu to Manila pass through Tagaytay, and from Talisay on the shore of Taal Lake, the Tagaytay–Talisay Road climbs about
12km
up to Rotonda.
From Laguna: Jeepneys run up the Santa Rosa–Tagaytay Road from the Balibago terminal in Santa Rosa, and vans to Tagaytay leave from Calamba.
Jeepneys run along the ridge road with a base fare of about
. For short distances use a tricycle (about
, negotiable), and if you want to visit several attractions, chartering a tricycle by the hour (about
per hour) is convenient.
November–March
is best. Especially in
December–February
, morning temperatures can drop to 17–20°C, cool enough for long sleeves, and clear skies make the volcano view vivid.
March–May
is Manila's hottest stretch and draws crowds seeking cooler air, but even Tagaytay can reach 28–30°C at midday.
During the
June–October

rainy season, afternoon rain is frequent and thick fog often blankets the ridge, hiding the lake and volcano entirely on many days. When typhoons pass through, strong winds can topple trees or cause power outages. If visiting during the rainy season, plan to catch the view early in the morning.
Check Taal Volcano's alert level too. As of summer

, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) maintains Alert Level 1 (low-level unrest), with occasional minor steam explosions. If the alert level rises or volcanic gas (vog) thickens, those with respiratory conditions and young children should postpone their visit.

During the Christmas season and Holy Week, pilgrims visiting the convents and retreat houses join the vacationers escaping the heat, so room rates go up and the ridge road is jammed all day. Holy Week in
falls on
March 21–28
; during this period and other holidays, visit on a weekday or book your lodging early. During
October–April
the northeast wind blows steadily, and many people fly kites in the ridge-top parks.

Lodging along the ridge road ranges widely — lake-view hotels, garden-style resorts, guesthouses, and Airbnbs. A mid-range hotel with a lake-view room runs about
a night, an upscale resort about
, and a simple guesthouse about
. Rates rise and rooms sell out quickly on weekends and holidays, so book ahead. Since temperatures drop at night, it matters more to check for hot showers and thick blankets than air conditioning.

The staple food here is bulalo. Around Mahogany Market, restaurants that simmer bulalo with beef fresh from the butcher cluster together, and the long-running bulalo restaurant Leslie's is known for its lake-view seating. For a special occasion, Tagaytay's signature fine-dining restaurant Antonio's is popular, while the garden cafe Bag of Beans is a favorite for something more casual. Sonya's Garden in nearby Alfonso has long been loved for its organic salad and pasta courses. For a snack, try warm buko pie and fried tawilis, a freshwater fish from Taal Lake.

The area around Rotonda and Olivarez is close to bus stops and malls, making it convenient for travelers using public transportation, while the Tagaytay–Nasugbu Highway to the west is lined with hotels offering lake-view rooms, such as Taal Vista Hotel, along with Sky Ranch and Mahogany Market. The Tagaytay–Calamba Road side to the east is close to Picnic Grove and People's Park, and if you want a quiet garden-style stay, look for B&Bs in neighboring Silang, Alfonso, and Amadeo. Among restaurants, Balay Dako, a Filipino restaurant opened by the Antonio's group in a lake-view mansion, is also popular. Neighboring Amadeo is a coffee-growing town known as the "Coffee Capital of the Philippines," so local beans are easy to find at Mahogany Market and souvenir shops. Tawilis is a freshwater sardine found only in Taal Lake, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) listed it as endangered in
Roads into Tagaytay get extremely congested on weekends and holidays. Leave before
6 AM
or visit on a weekday.
The volcano view is clearest in the morning. Clouds and fog often roll in during the afternoon, so schedule your view cafe visit for the morning.
Mornings and evenings are cool, so bring a light long-sleeved layer or windbreaker, and a light jacket for
December–February
Bulalo portions at Mahogany Market are large, so it's normal for two or three people to share one pot. Check the size and price before ordering.
Large malls and restaurants take cards, but markets, tricycles, and street stalls are cash only. There's an ATM at the mall near Rotonda.
Good photo spots are the hill with the statue of Our Lady at People's Park, the Sky Ranch Ferris wheel, and the window seats of ridge-top cafes.
Grab is scarce and waits can be long, so if you're a group, a chartered vehicle with driver is the most efficient option.
Popular restaurants can have long waits at weekend lunch, so an online reservation is worthwhile.
Opening hours: Picnic Grove
, People's Park in the Sky
, and Sky Ranch
on weekdays and
on weekends and public holidays. Sky Ranch ride-all-day passes are cheaper online than at the gate, but the
admission is paid separately.
At the Pink Sisters Convent chapel and retreat houses, avoid sleeveless tops, shorts, and hats, and once inside, switch off your phone and camera and stay quiet.

Taal Volcano Island is a permanent danger zone designated by the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology, and landing on it is prohibited. Don't respond to touts on the lakeshore offering "volcano island tours." The institute also advises that boat trips and stays on Taal Lake should not be allowed.
If the alert level rises or a volcanic gas warning is issued, close windows, reduce outdoor activity, and wear an N95 mask if needed.
The ridge road has narrow sidewalks and fast-moving traffic in many stretches, making walking dangerous. Use a tricycle even for short distances.
Visibility while driving is very poor on foggy evenings. If you're driving yourself, get through the mountain road sections before dark.
During the rainy season and typhoon period, landslides and fallen trees can block roads, so check the weather forecast.
The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) is still keeping Taal Volcano at Alert Level 1 as of
September 2026
, recording steam emissions and volcanic earthquakes. Level 1 does not mean the risk of eruption has disappeared, so check the daily volcano bulletin on the
official PHIVOLCS website
Taal Volcano's alert level and the accessible zones change frequently. Be sure to check the official announcements of the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) before you go.
